oneSentence: A very large text-processing model predicts likely next pieces of language from a prompt and uses that pattern-matching ability to generate or transform text.
plainExplanation:
A large language model, often shortened to LLM, is a type of language model trained on very large amounts of text. “Large” usually refers to its scale: many model parameters, meaning many adjustable numerical settings learned during training, and often very large training data and computing effort. “LLM” is the acronym; “LLMs” is simply the plural.

What goes in is text, broken into small units called tokens. A token may be a whole word, part of a word, punctuation, or another short text fragment. The model reads the prompt token by token, uses patterns learned during training, and estimates which token is likely to come next.

What happens inside is not a database lookup and not human-style understanding. The system computes probabilities across many possible next tokens, then selects one according to its settings. It repeats that process again and again, so one token leads to the next until it produces a completion such as an answer, summary, translation or draft.

What comes out is generated text that may be useful, fluent and well structured, but it can still be wrong, invented or misleading. An LLM is the underlying model, not necessarily the full product a person uses. A chatbot or AI assistant may contain an LLM, plus extra parts such as instructions, safety rules, tools or document retrieval.

everydayAnalogy.title: Tuning a radio and filling in a weak sentence
everydayAnalogy.story: Amina and Luis are in a car driving between Nairobi and Arusha, and the radio signal keeps fading. They hear most of a news sentence clearly, but a few words are lost in static. Using the words before and after the gap, they make a best guess about the missing phrase so the sentence sounds complete. As more of the sentence arrives, they keep adjusting their guess one piece at a time.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A radio listener is trying to recover words that were actually spoken, while an LLM usually generates new text rather than restoring an original hidden sentence. Also, people bring real-world knowledge and intentions to the task; the model mainly applies statistical patterns from training and the current prompt.

visual.title: How an LLM turns a prompt into generated text
visual.learningObjective: After viewing this, a reader should be able to say that an LLM reads tokenised input, predicts one likely next token at a time, and repeats the process to build an output.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow diagram with four boxes connected by arrows. Box 1 shows a user prompt as a short sentence. Box 2 shows that sentence split into token chips. Box 3 shows the model assigning probabilities to several candidate next tokens, with one highlighted as selected. Box 4 shows the growing output sentence, then a loop arrow from Box 4 back to Box 3 labelled “repeat until stop”. Use plain rectangles, token chips and percentage bars in SVG; no decorative icons.

steps.label: Prompt enters
steps.explanation: The process starts with text from the user or another system.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box labelled “Prompt” containing the text: “Summarise this meeting in 3 bullet points.”

steps.label: Text becomes tokens
steps.explanation: The text is split into smaller units the model can process.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a second box labelled “Tokens” with separate rounded chips such as “Summ”, “arise”, “ this”, “ meeting”, “ in”, “ 3”, “ bullet”, “ points”.

steps.label: Next-token probabilities
steps.explanation: The model calculates which next token is more or less likely in this context.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a third box labelled “Candidate next tokens” with four horizontal bars: “-” 42%, “The” 21%, “1.” 18%, “In” 9%, with one option highlighted as selected.

steps.label: Output grows and repeats
steps.explanation: The selected token is added to the text, then the model predicts again until it reaches a stopping point.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a fourth box labelled “Growing output” showing text building step by step, such as “- Budget approved …”, and add a loop arrow from this box back to the probability box labelled “repeat”.

visual.interaction: On hover or tap, each step highlights and reveals one sentence of explanation; a play control animates the addition of two or three example tokens before stopping.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This diagram explains an LLM as a four-step flow. First, a text prompt enters the system. Second, the text is split into smaller units called tokens. Third, the model scores several possible next tokens and chooses one based on those scores and settings. Fourth, the chosen token is added to the output, and the same prediction step repeats until the text is complete. The main lesson is that generation happens incrementally, one token at a time, rather than all at once.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static four-box flow is shown instead of animation. The final box contains three successive output states side by side, for example: “-”, then “- Budget”, then “- Budget approved”, to show repeated token addition without motion.

workedExample.scenario: A student asks for a shorter version of a paragraph about urban heat.
workedExample.input: Prompt: “Summarise in one sentence: Cities often feel hotter than nearby rural areas because concrete and asphalt absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night.”
process: The prompt text is split into tokens and passed into the model.
The model uses the prompt context to estimate likely next tokens for a summary-style answer.
It generates tokens step by step, for example beginning with “Cities”, then “ are”, then “ often”, then “ hotter”.
After enough tokens form a complete sentence, the generation stops.
workedExample.result: Possible output: “Cities are often hotter than nearby rural areas because built surfaces store heat and release it slowly.”

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: An analyst in a UN office wants a first draft summary of non-sensitive, already-cleared incident trend notes to prepare for a meeting on protection patterns.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: This is relevant because an LLM can quickly turn large amounts of approved text into a shorter draft, helping staff review themes before human validation.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not paste confidential, personal, survivor, witness, security-sensitive or operational information into an unapproved public AI service; use only approved systems, minimise data, and keep human review in charge of any conclusions.

whyItMatters: Non-specialists make better choices about procurement, risk, policy and daily use when they know that an LLM is a pattern-based text generator, not a guaranteed source of truth or a complete product by itself.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: An LLM is the same thing as a chatbot.
commonMisconceptions.correction: A chatbot is an interface or product for conversation. It may use an LLM underneath, but it can also include retrieval, safety filters, memory, tools and workflow logic.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Because the text sounds confident, the output is probably correct.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Fluent wording comes from learned language patterns, not from automatic fact-checking. The model can produce false or invented statements that still sound convincing.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Large means it has simply stored the whole internet and looks up sentences.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Training adjusts many numerical weights so the model captures statistical patterns. It does not work like a normal search engine or exact phrase archive, though memorisation can occur in some cases.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: LLMs understand language in the same way people do.
commonMisconceptions.correction: People often use “understand” informally because the outputs can be coherent, but the mechanism is token prediction from learned patterns. Whether that counts as understanding in a stronger sense is debated, and the term can mislead.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: An LLM is a very large text model that reads a prompt and generates likely next pieces of text until it forms an answer.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: An LLM is a large-scale language model with many learned parameters that processes token sequences and generates a completion by repeatedly estimating a probability distribution over the next token and sampling or selecting from it.

keyTakeaway: An LLM produces text one token at a time from learned patterns, so it can be useful without being reliably correct.

quickCheck.question: Which statement best describes an LLM?
options: A search engine that retrieves exact stored sentences from a database
A large language model that predicts likely next tokens to generate or transform text
A chatbot interface with a human operator behind every answer
A fact-checking system that verifies each sentence before showing it
quickCheck.explanation: The core mechanism is next-token prediction over tokenised text. Some products built around LLMs may also search documents, use tools or apply checks, but those are additional components, not the definition of an LLM itself.
